truths.CP2:
WITH churned AS (
  -- one row per account and month from February to September 2025 in which it churned
  SELECT b.account_id
  FROM mrr_monthly AS b
  LEFT JOIN mrr_monthly AS m
    ON m.account_id = b.account_id
   AND m.month = CAST(b.month + INTERVAL 1 MONTH AS DATE)
  WHERE b.month >= DATE '2025-01-01'
    AND b.month <= DATE '2025-08-01'
    AND m.account_id IS NULL
)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) AS churned_accounts
FROM churned
truths.CP4:
WITH accounts_at_start AS (
  -- one row per account and month from February to September 2025: the account had MRR on the last day of the month before
  SELECT account_id,
         CAST(month + INTERVAL 1 MONTH AS DATE) AS month
  FROM mrr_monthly
  WHERE month >= DATE '2025-01-01'
    AND month <= DATE '2025-08-01'
)
SELECT ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN m.account_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS logo_churn_pct
FROM accounts_at_start AS s
LEFT JOIN mrr_monthly AS m
  ON m.account_id = s.account_id
 AND m.month = s.month

CP1.explanation: A churn rate asks what share of the accounts that began March were gone by its end, so the base is the accounts with MRR on 28 February; the end of March leaves out the leavers and adds the new accounts.

CP5.explanation: The table counts accounts, so it shows when churn peaked but not the MRR lost or why; the price rise is a cause to test by segment and plan, and a few percent a month adds up to far more over a year.
